time.verified_summary: Stock HiGHS 1.16.0 presolve takes 353.5 s summed over the 31 dev-size instances (median 4.29 s, geomean 2.42 s, SGM(0.1) 2.72 s, SGM(1) 3.95 s, maximum 139.4 s on rd-rplusc-21; SGM(0.1) per band A1 0.20, A2 0.56, A3 2.26, B1 16.86, B2 8.19, B3 10.27 s), and the patched build does not distort: presolved sizes identical on 31 of 31, diag/stock time ratio 0.949 to 1.050 with median 1.001. Size explains about half of the variation (time = 4.3e-6 * nnz^1.01 s, R2 0.51, residual factor 4.3x); 11 instances are more than 3x above the robust trend (rd-rplusc-21 61x, piperout-d27 25x, satellites2-60-fs 12x, sorrell3 11.5x, ravan 10.5x, var-smallemery-m6j6 9.4x, supportcase6 8.0x, unitcal_7 6.3x, splice1k1 4.9x, bab6 4.8x, tutaki 3.9x), while setup, initial scan, shrink and scaling follow size (R2 0.81). The time is concentrated: parallel rows/columns 32.2%, probing 22.0%, fast loop 17.7%, dominated columns 12.0% of the 349.8 s diag sum, and ten stage runs above half of an instance above 2 s hold 201.3 s (58%). rd-rplusc-21 spends 93.9 s in parallel rows (hashing 0.14 s) and 38.3 s in the fast loop, and with only the Stage 1 rules on it still takes 122.4 s (92.3 + 29.9 s): at least 69 s are in the call that deletes the 71,300 duplicate rows, and after that at least 21.6 s pass in which the fast loop and the next parallel-rows call remove no row; the source walks whole columns on single-nonzero events and this model has a column in 119,267 of 125,899 rows, but which code path runs is a hypothesis. Dominated columns take 28.5 s on tutaki and 9.9 s on supportcase6 and fix nothing (41.9 of the stage's 42.1 s have no yield); on tutaki the stage runs after the duplicate rows are gone, on 5,593 rows and 1.98 million nonzeros with 802 columns above 1,000 entries (longest 1,394), not on the original structure, and the number of pairs it tests is not in the data. tutaki's parallel rows need 9.26 s (8.85 s row loop) to delete 1,389 rows that carry 1,964,044 nonzeros, 99.6% of what the instance loses. Probing is slow for three reasons: splice1k1 (18.6 s) runs 1,001 probes of 0.95 matrix passes each and finds nothing because the limit counts probes; var-smallemery-m6j6 (16.9 s) spends 95% of 1.9e9 work units re-scanning about 157 rows of 1,400 to 2,300 entries that hold the one column with an infinite bound; piperout-d27 (12.2 s) is productive (2,816 columns, 38% of those removed), and satellites2-60-fs and unitcal_7 pay 70 and 93 ns per work unit against 9 to 11 ns, for a reason the patch does not measure. On sorrell3 clique merging is 8.3 of 10.4 s, of which 6.4 s are two repeated calls that change nothing; over all instances 7.95 of 12.03 s of clique merging are in such calls. On ravan the fast loop (10.3 s) removes at least 136,705 of its 148,567 rows in at most 2.6 s, and with only Stage 1 rules it removes 159,571 rows in 2.24 s, so the remaining 6 to 8 s appear only with the aggregator, sparsify, dominated-column and enumeration stages on, not through long columns alone. In total 87.9 s (25.1%) are in reduction-stage runs that removed nothing (dominated columns 41.9, probing 27.3, strengthening 6.7, enumeration 5.6, fast loop 4.2, parallel rows 1.4 s), 8.6 s in runs that removed almost nothing and 4.0 s in runs that only tightened bounds, and about 44 s more without yield sit inside runs counted as productive. HiGHS restricted to the Stage 1 rule set is measured in the supplement run diag_stage1: 164.6 s summed (122.4 s rd-rplusc-21), SGM(0.1) 0.650 s overall and 0.064 / 0.086 / 0.244 / 2.52 / 1.70 / 4.65 s for A1 to B3, well below the stage sums of the full run (0.971 s overall). For the design: per-event column walks, uncapped pair tests, repeated merges, a probe-count limit, full scans of one-infinite-term rows and re-sorted covers are costs an algorithm removes without a GPU; inherent work is productive probing (2.9e8 to 1.9e9 entry updates), the first clique merge and the passes over the model, for which HiGHS pays a median 113 ns per nonzero in setup and 292 ns per row-and-column scan.
verified_design_implications: Baseline and shift for the time target: stock SGM(0.1) per band A1 0.196, A2 0.564, A3 2.263, B1 16.86, B2 8.19, B3 10.27, all 2.725 s. Use the 0.1 s shift: 9 of 31 instances run below 0.3 s and 11 below 1 s. Anchors for the 'small constant': diag against stock differs by up to 13.4 ms below 1 s; 20% of the fastest instance (0.083 s) is 16.6 ms = 1,844 kernel launches at 9.0 us or 1,201 kernel-plus-read-back steps at 13.8 us. Multi-second stage times repeat within about 4% over five runs of the patched build.

Stage 1 gate reference: use the restricted run, not stage sums. HiGHS with only the Stage 1 rules (diag_stage1): SGM(0.1) A1 0.064, A2 0.086, A3 0.244, B1 2.521, B2 1.697, B3 4.654, all 0.650 s; medians 0.050 / 0.083 / 0.274 / 1.719 / 2.030 / 4.211 s. Caveats: one run, parallel jobs not recorded in the summary, and the fast loop still holds some Stage 3 column rules. Repeat it with --jobs 1 before the constants are fixed.

Aggregates are carried by a few runs. Full presolve: ten stage runs hold 58% of the summed time, four of the five B1 instances have a dominant-stage excess. Stage 1 reference: rd-rplusc-21 is 122.4 of 164.6 s; B1 SGM(0.1) is 2.52 with it and 0.90 without. A shifted geomean below HiGHS can be reached without being faster on ordinary instances, so gate also on the median per band and on the per-instance ratio.

Row deletion and the pass after it must cost time proportional to what is deleted. Evidence: rd-rplusc-21 needs at least 69 s to delete 71,300 seven-entry rows and then at least 21.6 s in which no row goes; tutaki needs at least 7.8 s for 1,389 rows. HiGHS's own cost without long columns is the reference: cygnet deletes 2,449,451 nonzeros in a 0.53 s row loop (0.22 us per nonzero), which would be 0.11 s for rd-rplusc-21 and 0.43 s for tutaki. Requirement to add to section 2.3: no implied-bound, dual-bound or change-mark update loops over a column or row per event; they are applied once per round over the affected rows and columns. That the HiGHS cost is the markChangedCol walk is a hypothesis.

Pairwise dominated columns (Stage 3) need a hard work cap and a filter that survives long columns: 41.9 of 42.1 s are runs that fix nothing (tutaki 28.5 s, supportcase6 9.9 s), the five productive runs take 0.21 s together, and predictive bound analysis strengthened no bound on any instance. Requirements: budget in column-entry comparisons as a function of nnz; cap or skip a column whose shortest row is long; a signature wider than 32 bits (saturated on tutaki by columns of 840 to 1,394 entries at stage time); implied-bound test once per column. Print HiGHS's numDomChecks before sizing the cap: the pair counts are not in the data.

Probing needs a work budget in entry updates and a yield-based stop: splice1k1 pays 952 x nnz in 1,001 probes for nothing, productive runs range from 20 x nnz (supportcase7, 5,193 columns) to 2,230 x nnz (var-smallemery-m6j6, 1,021 columns), so a fixed budget alone does not separate them. Stop a pass when a set amount of work passes without a finding; re-probe only sources whose neighbourhood changed (piperout-d27 round 4: 3.4 s and 5,783 probes for 22 columns; var-smallemery rounds 2 and 3: 7.8 s for 14 substitutions).

Rows with exactly one infinite activity term must cost constant time per touch in propagation: var-smallemery-m6j6 spends 1.8e9 of 1.9e9 work units scanning about 150 rows of 1,779 to 2,820 entries to find the one infinite entry. Keep, per row and side, the position of the single infinite entry (or find it only when the count becomes one), next to the exact counters of section 2.4.

Clique work: merge only cliques that changed since their last merge. HiGHS spends 7.95 of 12.03 s of clique merging in calls that change nothing (sorrell3 6.4 of 10.4 s). The first merge (sorrell3 1.95 s for 169,162 edge rows to 2,703 cliques; savsched1 154,995 rows deleted) is the inherent work. Bound the explicit pair store: HiGHS adds 1.0 to 1.2 million two-entry cliques, all pairs without a common clique, in 848 and 60 probes on satellites2-60-fs and supportcase6, stops on its clique limit and pays 0.63 to 0.68 s to rebuild the table. Whether those pairs are used later is not measured.

Per-pass constants to beat: HiGHS pays a median 113 ns per nonzero for setup, 292 ns for one row-and-column scan, 61 ns per parallel-rows hash pass and 94 ns per probing preparation, and repeats shrink, matrix rebuild and propagation at every enumeration and probing call. On band B3 setup plus first scan is 0.8 to 2.1 s; on band A one scan is 0.015 to 0.18 s. A device pass has a fixed cost of 9 us per launch and 14 us per read-back; a reduce over 1e7 values takes 94 us. Use a per-nonzero hash of constant cost (HiGHS does a modular exponentiation per nonzero).

The fast loop needs a cost that follows its frontier. Its cascade is cheap where it works (supportcase12: 1.8 million nonzeros in 1.08 s; ravan with Stage 1 rules only: 159,571 rows in 2.24 s), but HiGHS pays 2.75 s on bab6 and 0.82 s on cygnet for no removal, at least 21.6 s on rd-rplusc-21 after a mass deletion, and 6 to 8 s more on ravan once aggregator, sparsify, dominated columns and enumeration are on. Before Stage 3, measure per-call fast-loop time in HiGHS to find which stage triggers the ravan cost.

Inherent work where the GPU has to win by width: productive probing (piperout-d27 2.9e8 entry updates for 2,816 columns, 12,801 rows left without probing against 7,094 with it; var-smallemery round 1; supportcase7; bab6; unitcal_7 with 100 dependent sweeps of 4 rows per probe, which pays on a device only when all sources are batched), the first clique merge, and the passes over the model.

Every stage needs a bounded cost when it yields nothing: 87.9 s (25.1%) are stage runs that removed nothing (dominated columns 41.9, probing 27.3, strengthen inequalities 6.7, enumeration 5.6, fast loop 4.2 s) and about 44 s more lie inside productive runs. For Stage 4, cover strengthening must sort a row once and keep the cover incrementally: bab6 pays 1,565 ns per nonzero and call (4.0 s) for no strengthened coefficient.

claims_found_wrong.claim: Each binary that a probe implies is added to the clique table as a two-entry clique (skipped only when the clique table itself gave the implication or the table is over its entry limit), also when the implication comes from a set-partitioning or cardinality row that already is that clique; design implication: do not store row-implied literals as explicit edges
claims_found_wrong.correct: HighsImplications::computeImplications skips an implied bound only when its reason is the clique table AND (it comes from the probed column's own cliques OR the table holds at least 100,000 + nnz entries). Every other implied binary is passed to HighsCliqueTable::addClique, which stores nothing when the two literals already share a clique (haveCommonClique, then 'if (!hasNewEdge && origin == kHighsIInf) return'). So a literal implied by a row that is already a clique in the table is not stored again, and a cardinality row is not a clique. The 1.0 to 1.2 million new two-entry cliques on satellites2-60-fs and supportcase6 are pairs without a common clique. What the data supports is a cap on the explicit pair store, not that the pairs duplicate row cliques.
claims_found_wrong.how_checked: highs/mip/HighsImplications.cpp computeImplications (loop over domchgstack and the addClique loop); highs/mip/HighsCliqueTable.cpp addClique (lambda fixAllVarsInClique and the hasNewEdge test)

claims_unsupported.why: The analyst labels it a hypothesis and it stays one. analyst_findings.claim: The dominated-column stage compares every column j with every other column k of the shortest row that holds j with a positive coefficient and of the shortest one with a negative coefficient. A pair that passes a 32-bit row signature and the cost test is checked by walking column j with a search in the row tree per entry, then column k. The limit on the number of checks (300,000, then an average of 10,000 per column with at least 0.01 reductions per column) only stops columns that have neither an implied bound nor a clique; a column with an implied bound or in a clique is always compared with its whole shortest row. The implied-bound test is re-evaluated for every k. Cost term: sum over columns of the length of their shortest row, times the walked part of two columns for pairs the signature lets through; a signature of 32 bits is saturated by a column with far more than 32 rows.

probing.verified_summary: On the 31 dev-size instances HiGHS probing takes 76.9 s of 349.8 s presolve (22.0%; 55.5% in band A, 18.1% in band B), 84% of it in the probing loop, and 62% of it on three instances (splice1k1 18.6 s, var-smallemery-m6j6 16.9 s, piperout-d27 12.2 s); the enumeration stage before it takes 26.9 s (7.7%). 29 instances have candidates, 2,012,390 in round 1; HiGHS probes 40,577 of them in round 1 (2.0%; per-instance median 14.7%, below 10% on 12 instances, at least 95% on 4) and makes 66,435 probes over 47 rounds. The rounds end by the neighbourhood contingent (18), the probing contingent (9), all candidates visited (8), deletions (8), the clique limit (2) and no binaries (2). From the source and confirmed by the counts, the probing contingent is 1000 probes plus credits for reductions (six instances stop at exactly 1,001 probes), and the neighbourhood stop is in practice a cap on fruitless probes in a row of about sqrt(0.2 nnz): it gives the exact probe count on 7 of the 8 rounds that found nothing when the nonzero count at probing time is used, and it counts a probe that only stores implications as a failure (rmatr200-p5: 57,750 implications in 151 probes). One probe costs a median of 3,807 counted entries and 264 microseconds, from 18 entries (supportcase19) to 1,675,031 (splice1k1), with a floor of 16 to 44 microseconds per probe that the counters do not see; activity updates along columns are at least 80% of the counted work on 22 of 29 instances. HiGHS needs a median of 2.15 sweeps per probe and at most 201 (piperout-d27), but its sweeps count passes over model rows only, because clique and implication consequences are applied inside the bound change, so this is a lower bound for a design that propagates cliques in sweeps. Probing applies 12,230 fixings and substitutions, 90.9% of them on five instances, and 14 of the 29 instances get none. Measured by switching probing off, the presolved sizes are unchanged on 14 instances (28.3 s of probing; supportcase19 still differs in one column bound), probing saves at least 10% of the presolved nonzeros on six (rd-rplusc-21 56.9% from 17 fixings and substitutions) and 28.7 s of probing go to six instances that gain less than 1%. Clique merging deletes 325,724 rows, 98.7% on sorrell3 and savsched1, and 322,095 of them also with probing off; it costs 12.0 s, 8.0 s of that in calls that change nothing, and without it the presolved models have 326,072 more rows and 564,995 more nonzeros. Probing every round-1 candidate once is 2,012,390 probes; extrapolated from the probes HiGHS made that is 80.2e9 entries in HiGHS's count and 44.7e9 without the undo half (36.1e9 of it on supportcase6, from 60 probes), a time of that count divided by X, but these are counts of HiGHS's delta scheme, the per-probe work varies up to 12 times between rounds of one instance, and a scheme that recomputes touched rows has a different count that the patch does not record. What the unprobed candidates would yield is not in the data; it needs a run with HIGHS_DIAG_PROBING_NOSTOP=1.
verified_design_implications: Budget unit: count the probing budget in entries per nonzero, not in probes. HiGHS's 1,001 fruitless probes are 0.16 entries per nonzero on neos-5052403-cygnet and 952 on splice1k1 (18.2 s for nothing). By the extrapolation, about 100 entries per nonzero in HiGHS's count completes a pass on 18 of 29 instances; the five that need far more (splice1k1 1,547, bab6 1,896, var-smallemery-m6j6 2,326, satellites2-60-fs 5,142, supportcase6 61,790) include two where probing pays most, so the cap has to cut by candidate order inside an instance. Treat the per-instance figures as orders of magnitude: the mean work per probe moves up to 12 times between rounds of one instance.

Do not size the kernels from HiGHS's entry counts alone. They count column entries per bound change (a delta scheme); DESIGN.md section 2.4 recomputes each affected row over its entries, which costs row length per touched row and sweep. Add three counters to highs_diag.patch before the overlay is specified: bound changes per probe, distinct rows touched per probe, and the summed length of those rows. Until then the delta-or-recompute choice and the first kernel to build are open; the analyst's ranking (activity update before row evaluation) holds for the delta scheme only.

Per-probe cost spans five orders of magnitude (18 to 1.7e6 counted entries as instance means, a single probe up to 3.0e6 = 3.5 times the nonzero count), so slots must be balanced by work, a probe must be closable by a work cap and reported as capped. A fixed cost per probe matters as much as entries on the cheap instances: HiGHS pays 16 to 44 us per probe below 1,400 entries, and supportcase19 has 1.3 million candidates of 18 entries each.

Slot state needs both forms. Mean row-activity updates per probe value are at most 2% of the row count on 11 to 14 instances (presolved or original row count) and above the rows present on supportcase6 (146 x), splice1k1 (64 x), supportcase7 (4 to 8 x) and sorrell3 (7.9 x of the 2,701 rows left after clique merging), and above the presolved row count on var-smallemery-m6j6 (1.9 x) and rd-rplusc-21 (1.8 x). Choose per instance from a measured first batch.

Sweeps: bound a probe by work, not by a small sweep count (unitcal_7 needs a mean of 101 sweeps per probe and yields 312 fixings and substitutions). The fixed cost of deep probes is small per launch (201 sweeps x 13.84 us = 2.8 ms), but a launch lasts as long as its deepest slot: piperout-d27 has a mean of 2.5 sweeps and a maximum of 201, uccase9 2.4 and 66, so slots must be refilled or the tail handed to the host. HiGHS's sweep numbers leave out clique and implication chains, so the design's own sweep depth has to be measured.

Implicit propagation: on ns1208400, sorrell3 and sp98ar HiGHS counts no row entry at all while bounds spread (sorrell3 21,281 activity updates per value), which fits propagation through the clique table but is not recorded by reason. neos-5052403-cygnet has no clique at loop start and no row queued and still gains 13,552 cliques; the only source in the code is dual-fix probing (lock counts of rows that become redundant). Decide whether the probe kernel includes that rule; its cost is not in any counter.

The harvest must be bounded and compact: round means reach 19,635 new cliques per probe (supportcase6) and 3,800 new implications per probe (supportcase7 round 2); satellites2-60-fs, supportcase6 and bab6 produce 0.8e6 to 1.2e6 two-entry cliques from 60 to 2,500 probes, and on supportcase6 the presolved sizes do not change at all. Keep a cap of the kind max(1e6, 2 nnz) new items per pass and store implied binaries as one list per source.

Limits. Copy: the cap on new cliques and implications, the time limit, another pass only after the model changed. Artefacts of probing one column at a time: the probe-count contingent, the failure-run stop (it ends five band A instances after 71 to 151 probes and treats stored implications as failures), the deletions abort with its 2,500-probe switch, and probing every column again in a full round (piperout-d27 round 4: 22 reductions in 3.40 s, round 3 still 314 in 3.45 s). The batch equivalents are an entry budget, a yield test per launch, applying the harvest between launches and re-probing only sources whose neighbourhood changed. The candidate order is neither supported nor refuted by this data.

Do not rebuild the model before probing: HiGHS pays 0.84 to 1.12 s of preparation per probing round at 3 to 4.3 million nonzeros (61 to 95% of the probing time on kenana, kasavu, supportcase19) for no reduction. The same instances spend 1.23 to 2.63 s in the enumeration stage without a change of size; how much of that is the same preparation is not measured.

Clique gate of Stage 2, measured by removal: without clique merging the presolved models have 326,072 more rows and 564,995 more nonzeros, almost all on sorrell3 (166,461 rows, presolve then returns Not reduced) and savsched1 (154,995 rows); merging deletes at least 100 rows on 7 instances. It does not depend on probing: 322,095 of the 325,724 rows are deleted with probing off. Merging adds nonzeros on some instances (brazil3, piperout-d27, uccase9 have fewer nonzeros but more rows without it), so the gate has to count rows and nonzeros. Skip a merging call when the clique table has not changed since the last one: 8.0 of HiGHS's 12.0 s are calls that change nothing (sorrell3 6.4 s). Merged cliques also make probing cheaper (sorrell3: 936 against 15,317 us per probe).

Judge probing by the presolved model, not by counts: rd-rplusc-21 gets 17 fixings and substitutions and loses 57% of its presolved nonzeros when probing is off, while 28.7 s of HiGHS's 76.9 s go to six instances that gain less than 1%. The Stage 2 gate should compare the model after the whole presolve with and without the new probing, by rows, columns, nonzeros and bounds (equal sizes hid a changed bound on supportcase19).

Before the Stage 0 probing budget is fixed, run the 31 instances with HIGHS_DIAG_PROBING_NOSTOP=1 and a time limit, with the three extra counters: it replaces the one-pass extrapolation (81% of which is supportcase6, from 60 probes) by a measurement and gives the yield of the candidates HiGHS never probes.

What the clique table and the stored implications fix is applied recursively inside HighsDomain::changeBound (HighsCliqueTable::addImplications, HighsImplications::applyImplications) and adds no sweep; on the four instances with prop_entries = 0 the count is 0 or 1 sweep per probe although bounds spread (sorrell3: 21,281 row-activity updates per value). claims_unsupported.claim: The one-pass entry counts (44.65e9 without undo, 37 entries per nonzero in the median) are what a GPU pass costs; the kernel to design first is the activity update per (slot, column), not the row evaluation.
claims_unsupported.why: activity_entries is the column length per bound change: the count of HiGHS's scheme, which adds deltas along columns. DESIGN.md section 2.4 folds every affected row over its entries on the GPU; that costs the row length per touched row and sweep, and the patch counts neither bound changes per probe nor distinct rows touched. At least 61,832 are forcing-row fixings (Stage 1). A counter per calling rule around fixColToLower/Upper and removedFixedCol is the one patch addition that settles Stage 1 against Stage 3 (dominated columns, dual-fixing extension, stuffing).

Redundant rows are the largest row family (37.7%, at least half on 10 instances) and HiGHS tests them on implied-bound activity sums. Whether the plan's explicit-bound sum loses rows is not in the data; a patch switch that tests redundancy on the *Orig sums would measure it. Hypothesis until then.

Clique merging: measured effect of switching it off is 34.5% of the rows and 4.5% of the nonzeros; the result changes on 15 of 31 instances, rows are deleted on 12 and extended on 12, but only sorrell3 (everything), savsched1 (95.7% of rows, 92.6% of nonzeros) and var-smallemery-m6j6 (30% of rows) lose 10% or more. It needs no probe and no enumeration stage (same deletions inside the probing stage when enumeration is off), so the clique pipeline can be gated apart from probing. sorrell3's pairwise dominated columns depend on it.

Probing must be judged on the sizes after the cascade loop, not on its own fixings: without probing 43,899 fewer rows go, 86.9% of them in the fast loop (rd-rplusc-21 28,552, piperout-d27 3,871, supportcase7 1,681). For nonzeros half of the loss is the probing stage itself and a quarter is bab6's second sparsify call. HiGHS's probing limit leaves reductions: on kenana and kasavu a run that probes 7,867 / 11,766 times instead of 1,001 removes 34% / 42% more rows.

Stage 3 content by summed columns: dual-fixing substitution 62,194 (9 instances, ravan 51,601), zero-cost singleton 57,879 (3, supportcase12 57,541), simple probing on equations 13,874 (3, brazil3 13,782), aggregator 11,766 (17 instances, net fill-in 8,907), parallel columns 8,089, pairwise dominated 7,652 (5), singleton-column substitution 3,788 (13). By number of instances the order is aggregator, singleton-column substitution, dual-fixing substitution. Leaving out all stage-level Stage 3/4 and left-out rules while keeping probing and cliques costs 2.5% of rows, 3.0% of columns, 2.8% of nonzeros in sum, concentrated on trento1, satellites2-60-fs, bab6, supportcase6, piperout-d27. Forcing columns (4) and implied equations (22) can come last.

Sparsify is 2.7% of the nonzeros overall, 53.5% on bab6 and 27 to 31% on trento1, kenana, kasavu; on trento1 it (or the aggregator) also unlocks the parallel-row removal. Cover strengthening removes 144 nonzeros and can only be judged on the LP bound. Whether a second sparsify call without probing gains on bab6 is untested.

Left-out rules: direct cost 0.21% of rows and 0.18% of columns (Fourier-Motzkin 1,284 rows / 949 columns, VB aggregation 723 rows, enumeration-stage fixings 1,002). satellites2-60-fs is the exception and is not understood: Fourier-Motzkin removes 22.4% of its nonzeros directly, and with Fourier-Motzkin, aggregator, dominated and parallel columns, sparsify and enumeration off together HiGHS reaches only 15 to 20%. Run it with only fourier_motzkin off before deciding that an explanation line is enough.

Size comparison: use rows, columns and nonzeros together and report clique-extension nonzeros (189,101) and aggregator fill-in (8,907 net) apart. A restricted rule set can leave fewer nonzeros than HiGHS with more rows and columns (brazil3 101.9% of the nonzeros at 95.9% of the rows; unitcal_7 101.5% at 81.5% of the rows and 47.0% of the columns).

Quality next to size: report implied integers (8 instances; most of the non-integer columns left on trento1 and ns1830653, a third on tutaki) and row dynamism; HiGHS itself raises p99 27 times on ravan and 51 times on supportcase12, which matters for the plan's limit of 10 times HiGHS's value.

structure.verified_summary: The 32 instances need all three classes of the binned matrix, and the exact counts in the sweeps files show where the work sits: rows of at most 4 entries are at least half of the rows on 18 instances but hold at least half of the nonzeros on 7, rows above 64 entries hold at least half of the nonzeros on 14 and columns above 64 on 10 (18 in either orientation), rows above 8,192 exist on 5 (square47 1,360 rows with 87.7% of the nonzeros, supportcase6 15 with 40.1%, bab6 8 with 39.0%) and columns above 8,192 on 3 (rd-rplusc-21 9 columns with 69.8%, the longest 119,267 entries). One thread per row over the whole CSR is measured at 39.2 ms per pass on bab6, 34.9 on square47, 22.4 on supportcase6 and 20.0 on supportcase7 against 0.12 to 0.47 ms for the binned kernel (10 times or more slower on 13 of 32); up to 64 entries lane groups beat one thread per row on 23 instances (up to 2.5 times) and lose on 5 (by at most 27%), and the gather benchmark's 1.4 to 3.4 times covers rows of 4 to 64 entries only. Rows with exactly one infinite activity term occur on 21 of 32 instances; with the row-side counts the case is certain on a side the row has for at least 10% of the rows on 6 (rmatr200-p5 100%, trento1 99.8%, rd-rplusc-21 at least 95.4%, supportcase40 40.2%, unitcal_7 at least 35.0%, savsched1 at least 12.3%), possible on 11, and limited to 27.3% on kenana and kasavu; rows with two or more are at least 10% on 5 (supportcase42 94%); no instance has a finite bound of 1e8 or more and 6 have free columns. After stock HiGHS presolve 6 of 30 reduced instances keep a row with an infinite term, and 13 of 29 do in the run with enumeration and probing off (kenana and kasavu keep all 496,860 and 695,604 infinite upper bounds), which confirms that HiGHS makes implied bounds explicit in prepareProbing and nowhere else in that run. Clique rows are at least 10% of the rows on 15 instances; HiGHS's clique merging changed rows on 14 of 31 and at least 1% of the rows on 7, but sorrell3 (166,459 of 169,162 rows deleted, 80% of its presolve time in merging) and savsched1 (154,995 of 295,989) hold 98.7% of all deleted rows, and by the source a row is deleted either because its extended clique lies in another row's clique or because its clique lies in an extended one. HiGHS's explicit clique table reaches 0.57 to 1.18 million cliques on 4 instances and stops probing on its clique limit on 2; variable-bound rows are at least 10% of the rows on 5 instances, aggregation acts on 5 (uccase9 is in both groups) and removes at most 722 rows. Only rd-rplusc-21 has a row dynamism above 1e6 (1e7 raw, 1.8e5 with HiGHS's scaling, 5,750 after presolve); HiGHS presolve worsens the 99th percentile on 7 of 30 instances (more than 10 times on ravan and supportcase12), improves it on 4, and its p99 is 1 on 11, where our ceiling is 10. Ten instances are all-integer and 7 have under 10% integer columns; HiGHS's presolved model has implied integer columns on 8 of 31 (more than 100 on 6), and the same 8 have them in the stage-1-only run. Band A1/A2 models have 71K to 133K nonzeros, 1.3K to 49K rows and a median row of at most 4 entries on 8 of 11; 1% of HiGHS's presolve time there (0.083 to 4.28 s) holds 92 to 4,753 empty kernel launches (median 249), 60 to 3,096 rounds of one kernel plus a read-back (13.84 microseconds each) and 1 to 95 sorts of 1e5 keys. Measured on those matrices a full GPU round costs 62 to 103 microseconds against 305 to 740 on one CPU thread (at most 0.52% of HiGHS's time) and a GPU frontier pass costs 55 to 167 microseconds whatever its size against 1 to 3 (warm) for 1% of the rows on the CPU, so sweeps cannot pay there. HiGHS spends 14% to 82% of its band A time in enumeration and probing and its last probing round stops early on 10 of 11; the fixed-cost floor of its probes run as one batch of synchronised rounds is at most 2.2 ms (under 0.4% of its probing loop on 10 of 11, 4.2% on supportcase40), an idealised figure that rules out a launch or a sort per small step, not batched wide phases. Exact counts: classes up to 64 entries hold at least 99% of the rows on 12 of 32 instances but at least 99% of the nonzeros on 7; rows above 64 hold at least half of the nonzeros on 14, columns above 64 on 10; chunks on 8 (5 by rows, 3 by columns), with 87.7% of the nonzeros of square47, 40.1% of supportcase6, 39.0% of bab6 and 69.8% of rd-rplusc-21 (columns). Tune the 0-2 and 3-4 groups for launch efficiency and the block and chunk kernels for throughput.

One thread per row over the whole CSR is out at every size: measured 12.6 to 39.2 ms per pass on the five instances with a row above 8,192 against 0.12 to 0.47 ms binned, and still 2 to 5 times slower on band A instances whose longest row is 145 to 200 entries. Inside the classes up to 64 entries the choice is per kernel and size: for activities lane groups win on 23 of 32 (up to 2.5 times) and one thread per row wins on 5 (rd-rplusc-21, supportcase42, kenana, kasavu, rmatr200-p5); for the column candidates one thread per column wins on the 8 instances with 114K columns or more except ravan (up to 2.1 times) and loses on 20 (up to 4.8 times). Fix the thresholds from the sweeps files, not from the gather benchmark.

Bin rows and columns independently: on all 8 instances with a chunk-class row or column the other orientation is short (at most 1,850 and 180 entries). The claim that counts on such rows must be reduction trees is not supported: the atomic-count activity kernel is within 0.89 to 1.11 of the reduced-count one and slower only on supportcase42. No measurement exists for a single column of 119,267 entries handled by one thread; none is planned either.

Upload after the first host cascade. The measure is the stage-1-only HiGHS run, not the share of trivial rows: Stage 1 rules alone remove at least half of the rows on 9 of 31 instances and at least half of the nonzeros on 10. Expect the length classes to shift afterwards (rd-rplusc-21 longest column 119,267 -> 47,974 stage-1-only and 19,355 full; supportcase7 longest row 24,039 -> 5,388) but not to vanish: after full HiGHS presolve rows above 8,192 remain on 3 instances and columns above 8,192 on 2.
Clique extension moves rows across length classes (sorrell3 2 entries -> median 37, maximum 71; savsched1 p99 16 -> 102), so the bins need a rebuild or an overflow path after the clique phase.

Keep the single-infinity rule in the Stage 1 propagation kernels: it applies for certain to 95% to 100% of the rows of rmatr200-p5, trento1 and rd-rplusc-21, to 40.2% of supportcase40, at least 35.0% of unitcal_7 and at least 12.3% of savsched1; on kenana and kasavu to at most 27.3%. The yield (bounds found) is not in any file. Exact uint16 counts cannot saturate on the 32 measured instances. The split layout S is not justified by skipped loads: it is within 1% of the paired layout on the five instances with many rows of two or more infinite terms.

Infinite-term handling is a Stage 1 requirement, not a corner case: a HiGHS restricted to Stage 1 rules keeps a row with an infinite term on 13 of 29 instances (99% of the rows of kenana and kasavu, 78% of unitcal_7), because it tightens continuous column bounds only in prepareProbing. Our presolve should make recorded implied bounds explicit before the first wide phase, as planned; DESIGN section 6 should not say that HiGHS also does it at the end.

The testbed does not exercise huge finite bounds (none of 1e8 or more) and has free columns on 6 instances only, so the 1e20 rule, the huge-bound guards and the free-column rules must be covered by the test oracle.

Stage 2 gate for the clique items: merging changed rows on 14 of 31 instances, at least 1% on 7, at least 10% on 3 (sorrell3 100%, savsched1 68.9%, var-smallemery-m6j6 20.4%); without merging HiGHS ends with 169,162 instead of 2,701 rows on sorrell3 and 289,008 instead of 134,013 on savsched1. Extension and removal of dominated rows are one mechanism (a row goes because an extended row contains it), so build steps 4 and 5 together. sorrell3 is the instance to beat: 8.3 of 10.4 s inside merging, 6.4 s of it in two calls that change nothing.

When a gate compares with a restricted HiGHS, read the size from the DIAG total line: HiGHS returns the original model with status Not reduced when only clique merging removed rows (sorrell3 in the diag_stage12 run: 2,703 rows inside, 169,162 returned).

Clique storage: explicit lists do not scale. HiGHS holds 564,799 cliques from the 6,444 knapsack rows of splice1k1 (one per item; the implicit (row, start) form holds one sorted row each) and 0.9 to 1.2 million after probing on satellites2-60-fs, supportcase6 and bab6, and stops probing on its clique limit on two of them after 60 and 848 probes. The pipeline needs implicit knapsack cliques and a cap on probing-derived cliques that does not end probing.

Clique detection must run on the post-cascade model and on the binary part of rows with other columns: 10 instances have no packing or partitioning row in the original model, HiGHS has cliques on 5 of them before probing, and uccase9 and unitcal_7 gain 1,932 and 121 clique rows through presolve. Two-binary rows are at least half of the rows on sorrell3, var-smallemery-m6j6 and ravan. Set-covering rows, which the plan propagates implicitly, are at least 10% of the rows on 7 instances.

Leaving VLB/VUB aggregation out of the first versions costs little on this testbed: HiGHS removes 722 rows with it on rd-rplusc-21 and rewrites at most 119 elsewhere (5 instances), and does nothing on kenana and kasavu, where variable-bound rows are 70% of the rows.

Stage 1 gate: the implied-integer conversions of HiGHS's fast loop cannot be switched off and they are large: the stage-1-only run ends with 1,248 implied integers on trento1, 137 on ns1830653, 1,521 on uccase9, 1,773 on supportcase42, 2,559 on savsched1 and 1,400 on tutaki. A shortfall against restricted HiGHS on these six has to be checked against this Stage 3 rule first.

Numerics gate: HiGHS's presolved p99 row dynamism is 1 on 11 of 31 instances, so our p99 may be at most 10 there; HiGHS itself raises p99 27 times (ravan) and 51 times (supportcase12), so a rise is not by itself a defect. Apply HiGHS's scaling in the harness before comparing (it changes row dynamism on trento1, uccase9 and rd-rplusc-21). How often the pivot veto at 1e6 fires cannot be read from the original models; cover it with oracle cases and count it in Stage 3.

Bands A1 and A2: sweeps do not pay. A full GPU round saves 0.2 to 0.6 ms per call against one CPU thread (at most 0.5% of HiGHS's presolve) and a GPU frontier pass (55 to 167 microseconds) loses to the CPU below about 10% of the rows, so the cascade stays on the host; HiGHS's initial scan plus fast loop take 21 to 125 ms there, which is the time the host engine has to beat. 1% of HiGHS's time holds 1 to 8 sorts of 1e5 keys on 9 of 11 instances, so bins rebuilt by a stable sort can be rebuilt a few times per call, not once per round.

Probing in band A: HiGHS spends 14% to 82% of its presolve in enumeration and probing and stops its last probing round early on 10 of 11 instances, so wide probing is where the time and the surplus are. The fixed-cost floor of synchronised rounds is small when probes are batched (13.84 microseconds per round, 2.2 ms for all of unitcal_7's probes), but a round must carry more than 5 probes on unitcal_7 and 3 on supportcase40 to pay even at that floor, and unitcal_7 needs up to 156 rounds for one probe at 28 entries per sweep: deep, thin propagation chains go to the host continuation, and the engine threshold must see the depth, not only the batch size. The real per-round cost with compaction is 4 to 12 times the floor and is not yet measured for a probing kernel.

analyst_open_questions: Exact share of the nonzeros per length class and in rows longer than p99: the statistics have percentiles only. A per-class histogram (rows and nonzeros per class 0-2 ... above 8192, for rows and columns) from baseline_tool, or from the CSR dumps on the node, would replace the bounds of table 1d.

Single-infinity rule: the statistics have no cross-table of infinite-term count against the side the row has, and no file says how many bounds the rule yields. On 6 of the 10 instances with a share of 10% or more the certain lower bound is 0 (among them kenana and kasavu, where the counts coincide with the variable-bound rows). A counter per (row side, infinite-term count) in baseline_tool would settle on how many rows the case applies; the yield needs our own propagation or a HiGHS counter.

Only square47 of the 9 instances above 1e7 nonzeros has statistics. The longest rows of t11nonreg, neos-4535459-waipa, hawaiiv10-130, a2864-99blp and the others are unknown, so the statements on chunk rows, on uint16 count saturation and on the share of long rows do not cover bands C and D.

The gather benchmark covers rows of 4 to 64 entries only. Thread-per-row against lane groups for rows of 1 to 3 entries, and block against chunk kernels above 64, are not measured on the testbed matrices (the sweeps_check files are functional checks on a 673-nonzero model).

Where do HiGHS's non-row cliques before probing come from on bab6 (78,952 in the table against 19,868 clique rows and 848 knapsack rows) and neos-4647030-tutaki (5,600 against 1,400)? The files give the table size only; the binary parts of cardinality or mixed rows are a guess.

The matrix range of the scaled original is not in the statistics, so the rise on uccase9 (40,000 raw to 2,560,000 presolved) and unitcal_7 (1,000 to 128,000) cannot be attributed to HiGHS's column scaling or to its presolve.

The times of tables 3e, 6d and 6e come from one patched run per instance; their run-to-run spread is not known, and the patched and stock times differ by up to 5% on band A (trento1 0.280 against 0.267 s).

HiGHS's loop time per probe includes its clique-table and implication work (rmatr200-p5: 449 microseconds per probe for 2,853 entries), so the per-sweep and per-entry figures of table 6e overstate its propagation cost; the GPU kernel time per round is not measured at all, so table 6f bounds the fixed cost only.
